utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. This afternoon, we will hear the final argument from the Prosecution. Mr. Scott, you informed us that you have some procedural matters to address to the bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. President, Your Honours, good afternoon. Only one question, just as a procedural matter. The Chamber had indicated earlier that rebuttal might be allowed on Thursday in the Court's discretion. And I just wanted to be sure before we start our arguments, presumably for the benefit of all parties, that whether or not there will be rebuttal or the amount of rebuttal will not be a function of either party then reserving time. Do I understand that correctly? You are not asking -- in other words, Mr. President, you are not asking or suggesting, if I understand correctly - I'm asking to be corrected if I'm wrong - that in order for the Prosecution to have any rebuttal time, we would have to reserve some of our time today and take less time today. So I'd appreciate the Chamber giving us some guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that you have to finish your final argument today, and after hearing the rejoinder argument of the Defence side, you may be given an opportunity on Thursday morning for one hour for your rebuttal argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It is true to the Defence counsel. The Defence counsel, each party, will have one hour for the rejoinder argument. That's what we understand the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Defence has an objection. We were under the understanding that each party would give final statements Monday morning, Tuesday morning, Wednesday morning and Thursday morning. The Defence of Naletilic is disadvantaged because the Prosecution, we find, is allowed to commence their final argument Monday afternoon, will go to 7.00. And then we're made -- the defence of Naletilic is made to come in tomorrow morning at 9.00. We have just been handed two binders of documents. Our further understanding is that on Wednesday and Thursday, the sittings will be in the afternoon. We absolutely cannot understand why we are put at this disadvantage. We believe that it violates the equality of arms theory that permeates this Court, and we feel that we should be allowed to give our final arguments commencing at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. Why should we be put in this position and be disadvantaged? And we are disadvantaged if we are made to argue tomorrow morning at 9.00 after stopping at 7.00 tonight. It's just not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the Court scheduling has been arranged by the Registrar a long time ago, and if you have some objections, you should have raised that objection almost a month ago when the scheduling was issued and this Trial Chamber does not believe that any Defence counsel was put in that disadvantaged position because this trial has been going on for 14 months already and we have already received your final argument in written form. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, we didn't know -- we had no idea that this schedule placed us arguing at 9.00 a.m. on Tuesday, when all other arguments start at 2.15 in the afternoon until last Friday. Absolutely did not know it until that time. Came as a surprise to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, anyway, the scheduling arrangement made by the Registrar has been issued a long time before. I think that's just on your part for the ignorance of that scheduling order. Yes, Mr. Scott. You may start your final argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, counsel, ladies and gentlemen, on 17th of April, 1993, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was on the cutting edge of ethnic cleansing. Those are the words that I told you on the 10th of September, 2001, when we started this trial. And the evidence that the Prosecution has submitted in these past 14 months has confirmed and proven that statement and each charge in the indictment. For Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, the days previous to the 17th of April, 1993, must have been both heady and yet anxious. It was heady because here he was the tip of the HVO sword, months and even years of talk, of dreams of an independent Croatia, of a Herceg-Bosna either free of Muslims or certainly with the Muslims in their place, what perhaps just now become a reality. And here he was on the cutting edge. Tuta's friend and a man he admired, Mate Boban, together with the HDZ, HVO leadership, had made their plans. They had issued an ultimatum to the Muslims, submit to the HVO by the 15th of April or face the consequences. And here was Tuta first in Siroki Brijeg and then in Risovac, chosen to implement that HVO plan and to enforce the ultimatum in Herzegovina just as Kordic and Blaskic and others were about to enforce it in central Bosnia. It must have been heady and exciting. But Tuta must also have been anxious. There is evidence, indeed even from a Prosecution witness, that Tuta took care of his soldiers. Some might have described him at least in this respect as a soldier's soldier, or a soldier's commander. He tried to plan his actions and carry them out in a way to minimise danger to his own troops. He must have thought even then, What will happen in these next few days? Could he have expected that only one, two, or three days later, one of his most trusted deputies, Mario Hrkac, Cikota, would be killed and several others of his soldiers as well? There is no doubt that Tuta was a charismatic man and a leader of men. His soldiers admired him; they considered him a hero. He was an example to them. He was a role model. It is unfortunate that when -- what he so often modeled to them was brutal treatment of Muslim soldiers and Muslim civilians. Beating prisoners, repeatedly, in front of his men, in effect, showing them the way, giving his approval, expelling women and children, burning their houses, destroying their mosques. Could such conduct be wrong when their very own Tuta did it himself? After the attack on Sovici and Doljani was completed, many of the Muslim prisoners were taken to the Doljani fish farm which the Chamber has heard much evidence about. There, they were repeatedly beaten and abused by Tuta personally and again by his senior officers and soldiers. Tuta threatened prisoners with a pistol. They were told to lie down and kiss Croatian ground. Tuta's soldiers followed his example. Only a few weeks later on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, Tuta found himself once again leading the HVO charge in Mostar. Perhaps even by then, the HDZ and HVO leaders knew that Tuta was given to extreme, even criminal, conduct. But there was a plan and it had to be executed. And for such a plan, you need men like Tuta, for when you lose the dogs of ethnic cleansing you want your dogs to be the meanest ones around. On the 10th of May, at the tobacco institute in Mostar, Tuta stood victorious with other senior HVO leaders and received the captured and arrested Muslim men. Tuta swore at the Muslim prisoners, insulted their balija mothers. He personally beat one prisoner in the face with a Motorola radio, and once again, as before and as so many times thereafter, once again, his own soldiers followed suit. There was also another man who would play a key role in the HVO's continuing attacks and expulsions in Mostar and the surrounding areas, one of Mladen Naletilic's commanders, Vinko Martinovic, Stela. A Muslim prisoner told you that he was twice taken to the front line in Mostar to work for Vinko Martinovic's unit. On the first occasion, the prisoner was beaten by Martinovic who told him, "You will find out who Stela is." In the midst of brutal treatments of Muslim prisoners who were taken for forced labour at Stela's front line area on the confrontation line in Mostar, you heard that Vinko Martinovic, Stela, said to them, "Stand up, balijas. Do you know who you have come to work for?" In 1993 -- Mr. President, Your Honours, in 1993, both of these men must have been relatively pleased with their positions. Certainly, things could have been better but overall, they were both powerful men. Overall, in their respective areas, with Tuta's area being a bit broader, they were powerful men. They had the power indeed of life and death, of freedom or captivity, of keeping your property or having it taken. Even then, both Tuta and Stela certainly wanted all of the power but none of the responsibility. And that is what they still want today, none of the responsibility. The Prosecution submits, Your Honours, that based on the law and the evidence, and the evidence that you have received, Tuta and Stela must be held responsible. Mr. President, Your Honours, before continuing on and discussing the evidence, I will tell you a bit about the trial. Some information about the evidence in the case in terms of how the Chamber might consider it, and about the Prosecution's plan for this closing submission. As you know, the trial began on Monday, the 10th of September, 2001. The Prosecution case in chief was concluded on the 24th of January, 2002. The Prosecution called 56 witnesses live in court. In addition to that, and we would respectfully ask the Chamber not to forget other important evidence because the Chamber also admitted the testimony of ten what we have called transcript witnesses, ten witnesses, important witnesses, from other Tribunal cases, those transcripts are in evidence, just as if they had given their testimony in this case. Important witnesses like Robert Donia and Remi Landry and Charles McLeod and others. In addition to that, the Chamber will recall that there were 16 deposition witnesses, all of whom testified in proceedings that began here at the Tribunal on the 23rd of July, 2001, and continued until the 3rd of August, 2001. So the Chamber will see that in addition to the 56 witnesses that were called live by the Prosecution, there are 26 other witnesses whose evidence is a matter of record, and indeed that evidence has been included in the final brief that the Prosecution has submitted. A very brief word about the exhibits, as voluminous as they are. The Chamber may have wondered from time to time about the Prosecution's numbering and organisational system. It's actually relatively straightforward although I'm sure not executed perfectly. The documents have been organised and numbered in such a way, with a few errors that we have certainly found in the past months, so that the documents are arranged chronologically. It was that practice that led us sometimes to have to enter, delineate, if you will, numbers from 31 to 32, being 31.5 or 31.6. The point is this: That in the work that the Chamber and your staff has in front of you, if one of you, Your Honours, or your staff wants to review documents, for example, related to the -- related to April 1993, you can go to the binders and you should be able to find in chronological order from the 1st of April to the end of April, all the exhibits covering that critical period of time. There are two exceptions to that. Some, but not all, of the international armed conflict exhibits are IAC exhibits, were and are organised separately in two binders. Likewise, the presidential transcripts or the PT exhibits are also organised separately. In terms of this closing argument, Mr. President, the Prosecution proposes to conduct it in this way. Obviously I have started the closing and I will address most of my comments and arguments to the accused Tuta. Mr. Stringer will then pick up the closing argument and address most of his comments to the accused Stela, and he will also touch on the question of the participation of the Croatian army, or the HV, in Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of the international armed conflict. Then, Mr. President, I will again rise to my feet and address finally a bit more on widespread and systematic, what might be considered the broader international armed conflict in terms of the political aspects, and will then end, bring to an end, the Prosecution closing argument. Mr. President, you said a few days ago, on the topic of the closing arguments, you said we, that is, you the judges, will have our briefs, and there is no need to repeat everything that is in the brief. Of course that is true. And I can tell you, Mr. President and Your Honours, that the Prosecution has fully accepted your guidance. We will not in our closing argument follow the Prosecution brief to any great extent, although certainly of course, given that -- given the case and the evidence in the case, our positions and the comments that we make will certainly be similar to those stated in our brief. As the Chamber will know and I will say primarily for the benefit of the public gallery, and for those who may be watching elsewhere, it is impossible, of course, to tell the whole story and to cover 14 months of evidence in any detail in the approximately four hours, now less, that the Prosecution has been given for closing argument. So we will certainly make no attempt to do that, and I'm confident, Mr. President, Your Honours, that when Mr. Stringer and I sit down at the end of the day, there will be vast parts of the case which will not have been addressed. But of course, that is what the briefs are for. Instead, what the Prosecution will do or at least what I will do, Mr. President, in my part of the closing argument is to recall in large measure - this won't be my entire argument - but I will recall in substantial measure six important witnesses, only six, that will give the Chamber an overall, we believe and respectfully submit, feel of the case and a reminder of much of the evidence that you have heard. These six witnesses have a particular focus in some respects, and that is they tell us about the man Tuta, who he was, and what his role was, in the HVO's war on the Muslim people. We will call six witnesses. Mr. President, the Prosecution calls the Spanish battalion officer Witness LL. You will recall that Witness LL, a senior officer in the Spanish army, testified about having dinner at Andabak's house in Siroki Brijeg on the 5th or 6th of April, 1993, approximately, he said day or two before he finished his report which itself was dated the 7th of April, 1993. Witness LL told us, "A. Yes, I met the whole family of Ivan Andabak. I also met his friend and a friend who was very important to him, and that was Tuta. "Q. Who introduced to you Tuta at that dinner? "A. The formal introductions were made by Mr. Ivan Andabak. "Q. Can you tell the Chamber, please, how was it if you remember, what words did Mr. Andabak use in introducing Tuta to you and saying who he was? "A. Well, after all these years I cannot really repeat the words, but what he said, that this was a very influential person, both in the world of politics and in the world of economy, of business, and in military life. And that it was his commander, that he worked with him, and that he was first and foremost his friend. "Q. Just now you said that he was his commander. Please explain between these two individuals, Andabak and Tuta, who was whose commander? "A. During the conversation at that time, I understood that Tuta issued orders to Ivan Andabak, that he was the commander, that Ivan Andabak was the chief of his Special Forces but above him there was Tuta, who planned operations or perhaps made a recommendation regarding the instructions, regarding the operations. "Q. Did you come to know the business of operations, so to speak, for Tuta and Andabak in 1993? "A. Yes, I came to know both the building which housed Ivan Andabak's office, his headquarters, and another building. In the interests of time I will skip a few places in the transcript. "Q. Let me go back to what you observed about the relationship between Andabak and Tuta during that evening or any other time. When you saw the two of them interact with one another, can you tell the Chamber: Was one of them more deferential to the other? "A. Well, at the time regarding this kind of relationship, you know, you're at a dinner which is very agreeable and you don't notice much of the hierarchy. What I could see was the friendship which existed between Andabak and Tuta. As for the deference, I could see that he was very happy, that he was very happy, very glad to be with Tuta, to be his friend. I could see that. Tuta was very smart, very dignified, highly ranking socially, and quite evidently above Ivan Andabak's level." Witness LL went on to tell us how he learned much about Andabak and Tuta during that dinner conversation. And we asked him: "Q. Did Tuta himself tell you some of his personal history? Did he tell you in his own words about himself? "A. Yes. He in a way supplied me with a summary of the story of his life, why he was in that particular situation at that time. He created the impression of a man who had left all the commitments he had outside his country to come and help his country. He wanted to invest all his effort, all that he had to defend the cause of his country and the Croats. "Q. What did Andabak and Tuta say about their intentions? "A. Well, the future was clear at the time to them. They were fighting for a country where Bosnian Croats would predominate and their intention was to set up a Republic of Herceg-Bosna, expelling the Muslim people from the area. "Q. Sir, is that what Tuta and Andabak said, it was their intention, their purpose, to expel all the Muslims? "A. Yes. "Q. Was anything said about the role of Mostar in Herceg-Bosna? "A. Yes. To them, Mostar could serve as the capital of the republic, a very important one. It was for them the key city, and they disliked in a way, they disliked the presence of Muslims in the area and because of that, they wanted to try to take precedent and to get rid of the Muslim population in the area, to apply pressure to get rid of the Muslims in the area." Now, going back to Mr. Andabak, do you recall how Mr. Andabak referred to Tuta? Did he describe him in any military term or refer to him in any way as a superior? Well, tell us what he said. "A. Well according to a document that that was done after the dinner party a report I put forward, Mr. Tuta was a sort of chief instructor of Ivan Andabak and the forces under him. He was over him. This is what I understood from Mr. Tuta." During Witness LL's testimony and I think arising out of cross-examination, the Chamber may recall that it was put to Witness LL how Andabak viewed Tuta, again in a military capacity. And this answer was given. "A. Andabak told me that sometimes Tuta was addressed as force commander. He told me that when I asked him, Who was your boss? And Andabak told me it was Tuta. He told me this on many occasions." If I can have Mr. Bos's assistance, I'm going to put certain documents in the course of my comments on the ELMO. Mr. Bos, if I could ask to you please put Exhibit 327 on the ELMO, first page of it. Mr. President, Your Honours, some of these documents you will have in a binder that has been provided to you. Some of them have been reserved, if you will, only to be placed on the ELMO. So you will not have every document that I refer to but a number of them you will have and also on the ELMO. Mr. President, I can tell already that the time is going to move very quickly, and I think on this document, the Chamber will recall, this is the report that was prepared by Witness LL, giving a detailed account concerning the person Tuta, about his views, his past, and his intentions. And I submit -- the Prosecution submits that that report is consistent with what Witness LL himself told you and other evidence in the Prosecution case. And the Chamber will have that document of course at its full disposal. Witness LL went on to talk about the accuracy of the information; he was questioned about that. The Chamber may recall that he talked about corroborating the information, that indeed much of it came from either Ivan Andabak or from Tuta himself. He also talked about later seeing Mr. Naletilic at a military meeting at Medjugorje and that further confirmed his understanding of Tuta's military role. It was ultimately put to Witness LL, who stayed in Bosnia then from that April and before, until July. He continued to collect information during -- throughout that time and he testified ultimately that "At the end, he did not change his assessment one bit." Which in his words meant, "It was all accurate." Now, before I leave Witness LL and go on to another witness, let me highlight a part of Witness LL's testimony in response to questions from Judge Diarra. Judge Diarra asked, "Witness, you were told, we do not like the presence of Muslims. Now, first, under what circumstances were you told that and who was that who told you that, and did this mean the presence of Muslims in the city of Mostar or throughout Herceg-Bosna?" Witness LL said, "Yes, specifically that night of the dinner party, both Mr. Tuta and Mr. Ivan Andabak said that they were against Muslims in that city. And subsequently, later on, when talking to other brigade commanders with whom I had contact, he mentions hearing from other HVO commanders that there should be no Muslims in that area." Judge Diarra then followed up and said, "The city of Mostar or all of the parts of Herceg-Bosna?" And Witness LL said, "Not only the city of Mostar, because it is very difficult to find a Muslim family in Ljubuski or the interior. Perhaps there were people like that, perhaps there were still some people." The Chamber will also recall, gets into the evidence concerning Sovici and Doljani but another report by the Spanish Battalion, Exhibit 325 which I will ask Mr. Bos to put on the ELMO and I will read -- refer to just part, on page 5. This was a Spanish battalion report and of course, the Spanish Battalion was part of the United Nations protection force on the ground. And in their report, on the 21st of April, on page 5, in reporting on the attack on Sovici and Doljani, they said this: "The offensive is directed by a person of substantial political, economic, and military influence; someone who is tired of signatures and political treaties. Hence he has no wish to uphold the cease-fire agreement struck between the Armija and the HVO. This person is known as Tuta. He has chosen two collaborators he had with him in Operation Bura namely, Ivan Andabak and Brigadier Lasic." There are other aspects of Witness LL's testimony. He remembers running into Andabak on the 7th of May, 1993, unexpectedly in Mostar and the Chamber may remember Andabak was fully kidded out, some might say in the vernacular armed to the teeth. And when LL asked him what was this all about, Mr. Andabak said, "Heads will roll." Of course the attack on Mostar was a short time thereafter. Finally, one further comment from Witness LL. In fact, he saw Tuta and Andabak later, after this dinner party, and he was asked: "Q. During these continuing conversations, did Mr. Andabak say anything more to you, not only about his personal objectives but what the objectives of the HVO were during this time? "A. Yes. He told me that his objective was to try and get all the Muslims out and that this was being very difficult to do because he had not expected such resistance and he thought it would have been easier to do this. "Q. Did you see the man Tuta again? "A. Yes, I did. It's nothing that we had scheduled at all. It was a casual encounter in Siroki Brijeg on the street. I saw that he had a military uniform on. We had a brief conversation. I realised he seemed to be quite satisfied that the war had begun and that he expected the war to come to a successful end; namely, getting the Muslims displaced from the city of Mostar." The Chamber will recall the testimony of Witness O. Witness O, a political leader on the Muslim side, who told the Chamber about a conversation he had in late 1992 in a meeting involving Boban, Naletilic, and others and how Tuta at the very beginning of the meeting essentially seized control of the meeting by racial commentary, suggesting there were no such things as a Muslim people, there were only Serbs and Croats. So polarising the meeting at its very beginning that the meeting essentially came to an immediate end. Witness O was asked to look around the courtroom and say -- and asked,. "Q. Do you see that man? Do you see that man that made those comments to you in that day in Mate Boban's office in Grude in 1992? Do you see that man? "A. Yes, the accused Naletilic." The Chamber will recall the testimony of the Dutch ECMM officer, Major Van der Grinten who talked again about his experiences and his encounters with Andabak and Tuta. He told you how that even in the official ECMM briefings and the information, they were told early on who this man Tuta was. He was in charge of two special units with one commanded by Andabak and the other by Juka. The Chamber will recall it was Van der Grinten that took the Chamber at some length through an organisational chart, Exhibit 532.1, prepared by the Spanish Battalion, indicating the place of Mr. Naletilic on that chart. Again showing him to be in a position on the chart immediately superior to Juka Prazina on the one hand and Ivan Andabak on the other. Turning to Exhibit 484, a report that was shown to Mr. Van der Grinten and perhaps Mr. Bos can assist us with that, page 4, the last page of that report, under item 6, Assessment, Major Van der Grinten told us about a meeting he had with another senior HVO officer named Slavko Puljic, and as the basis of that conversation he made his report which is Exhibit 484, saying this: "Mr. Puljic seemed to be more friendly than his HVO colleagues, also more honest than them. We think he has told us the truth when talking about the paramilitary organisations inside or next to the HVO. These organisations are extremist and nationalist, usually full of criminals from all over the world. Their power is their money and their behaviour, worse than any other people. We had met some of these capos of these Mafias, Mr. Tuta, Mr. Andabak, Mr. Juka, et cetera, et cetera, and we had confirmed their high level in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO." The Chamber will recall - and again, Mr. President, I'm finding I must move very quickly - will remember Mr. Van der Grinten's chance encounter once again with Andabak at the end of June 1993, when Andabak was with a group of men at that time. And by Mr. Van der Grinten's account, Andabak was not only surprised but frankly angry to encounter Van der Grinten in that situation. Didn't want to be seen there. Didn't want international observers there. And of course, the Chamber will know that it was at the end of June and the 1st of July when the second major waive of expulsions in West Mostar started. Mr. Van der Grinten testified to seeing the Defence Minister, Bruno Stojic in Siroki Brijeg and seeing Tuta at the same time. The Prosecution submits, Your Honours, that that is one of the relationships that the evidence shows of a man, this man Tuta, in close association with the Minister of Defence, the HVO Minister of Defence, Stojic, part of the power structure, if you will, that Mr. Naletilic drew on. The Chamber will recall the testimony of the mufti of Mostar, Seid Smajkic. I would respectfully submit to Your Honours a brave man who came and testified publicly with no protective measures despite his high public profile, unlike so many others who came, on all sides in fairness to the Prosecution, from the Prosecution and the Defence, and asked to be protected, not Mr. Smajkic. Mr. Smajkic came in here without protection and told his story. And told a compelling story and one of the parts of his story that the Chamber will recall was that the man, one of his colleagues, one of his subordinates in the Islamic church structure, the imam, Kasim Mezit. He told you clearly how Kasim Mezit was taken to Siroki Brijeg, personally interrogated and abused by Tuta, with Tuta becoming so angry with Kasim Mezit, the imam, that he stabbed the man in the face with a pencil, piercing his cheek when Kasim Mezit would not write on a piece of paper what Tuta wanted. Finally, the Chamber will recall Sir Martin Garrod a senior ECMM diplomat who had an extensive exchange and meeting with Tuta. You will remember his testimony about that, his lunch on the 15th of August, 1993, in Siroki Brijeg. In which Tuta again perhaps ultimately ill advisedly but was quite candid in his views about describing his history, his thinking, and his intentions to Martin Garrod. Martin Garrod made a report on that - and I will just briefly put it on the ELMO, Exhibit 565.2 - memorialising his lunch with Mr. Naletilic. Mr. Naletilic characterised the Muslims as Islamic fundamentalists, they had to be stopped. Sir Martin said, "This Tuta was definitely charismatic but I would not trust him," and he didn't. And the further comments are there for the Chamber to see, but I'm afraid we simply don't have time to cover them in detail. You will recall that Sir Martin also told the Chamber a fair amount about Tuta's connections with Zagreb, about people like Susak, the Croatian Minister of Defence; about Mate Boban; about their close association, their close contacts and dealings with one another. And indeed it was Sir Martin who said, "Siroki Brijeg seemed to be sort of an HVO or HDZ power centre. So many of the important things happened there." Sir Martin told the Chamber -- I asked him, "How did many of the Bosnian Croats consider Tuta?" And he said, "I would say about 50 per cent of the Croats to them Naletilic was mythical -- well, not mythical but a hero of the war. And they regarded him with respect and awe." And as I said in my earlier comments, Mr. President, it's a shame -- the Prosecution submits, it's a shame that a man respected by so many, sets such a poor example for so many to follow. Now, there has been considering discussion in this trial about who Tuta was, and I would like to turn, Mr. President -- let's not ask the Muslims who Tuta was, because we all know what the Defence position will be on that. Let's consider, who did the HVO, who did the HVO say that Tuta was? And I would ask the Chamber to direct its attention with the assistance of Mr. Bos, if he could put a schedule that has been prepared on the ELMO. And again Mr. President, I'm not going to have time to simply read off all these entries but look at person after person after senior HVO official and what they knew -- who they considered Tuta to be. Actually, the very first one is not an HVO official. It was the Croatian Minister of Defence, Susak, himself. Tuta was regarded as the HDZ's leadership "person" for military activities in the area of Herceg-Bosna. He referred to Tuta's men. He described Andabak -- Mr. Susak described Andabak as Tuta's deputy. Bruno Stojic, the HVO Minister of Defence who I already mentioned; Marijan Biskic, the assistant Minister of Defence for the HVO for security, who was responsible for both the military police and the intelligence service SIS; Ante Roso, chief of the HVO main staff; Slobodan Praljak, chief of the HVO main staff; Milivoj Petkovic, chief of the HVO main staff; Zarko Tole, senior member of the chief of the HVO main staff; Miljenko Lasic, opera stiff zone commander, Zeljko Siljeg, operative zone commander; Ivica Lucic, head of the HVO intelligence service; Mile Curic, chief of the HVO operations and training. Ivan Andabak himself, what did he tell Witness LL? Tuta was my commander. Stanko Bozic, the HVO warden; Josip Praljak, the HVO deputy warden. Vinko Martinovic, Stela himself in his testimony in the Zagreb proceedings said: "Tuta was the commander of the Convicts Battalion, Tuta was his superior." Ivan Baga, HVO commander of the Posuska battalion. Stipe Pole, the commander of the Mijat Tomic third Brigade. 17 of the most senior commanders, including none other than the Minister of Defence of the Croatian republic, and they all considered Tuta to be the commander of the Convicts Battalion, all considered Tuta to be a key military player in the HDZ, HVO structure. Prosecution submits, Mr. President, they were not wrong. The evidence concerning, turning now to Sovici and Doljani, the events that occurred there from approximately the middle of April 1993 until early May. I'm going to ask Mr. Bos to put on the ELMO a chart that has been prepared simply as an aid, comparing in particular as a vehicle, if you will -- and this will be in the judges' notebooks, I hope, should be -- the Rados diary, Exhibit 926C and other documentary evidence in the case. And what the Chamber will see is a compellingly consistent story told by source after source, document after document, witness after witness, that interlocks into a single, cogent, compelling description of the events in Sovici-Doljani. And if time allowed, I would spend much more time going through these exhibits. The Chamber can move from the Rados diary column repeatedly to the other evidence column and see the interlocking evidence, to see how what is said in the Rados diary is reported elsewhere. It is all of a piece, Mr. President, Your Honours, it all tells a story of the man Tuta, who was responsible for the ethnic cleansing of approximately 500 women, children, and elderly from Sovici-Doljani, the imprisonment, interrogation, and mistreatment of approximately 100 Muslim men, the burning, not during -- not battle damage, Mr. President, but after the armed conflict, after the battle was over, the intentional torching of the Muslim houses, the intentional destruction of the mosque when they were dynamited and blown down. I only will have time if I can ask Mr. Bos to help me with Exhibit P333. Now, Mr. President, I submit that the documents concerning Sovici-Doljani are particularly powerful but again -- the Chamber will be able to - as I am already sure has - review those in more detail. For now, I only -- I select one document, Exhibit P333, the report from Mr. Rozic on this 23rd of April, 1993, and really, Mr. Rozic sums it all up. After the armed conflicts in the settlements of Doljani and Sovici, the interrogation and arrest of all members of the army was carried out and civilians were collected in several places. In total, we have 422 women and children and 25 military conscripts. About 94 military conscripts were transported to Ljubuski. Seven military conscripts who had been killed and were members of the BH Army from Sovici have been buried so far. The Chamber will recall, and the Prosecution submits, that at least four of the prisoners were executed behind the Sovici school. Returning to Rozic's report: "After the conflicts in these areas ended, all Muslim houses were burned and two mosques destroyed at the order of high-ranking commanders." Who were those high ranking commanders, Mr. President? Judge Clark? Judge Diarra? The high ranking commanders, the highest of those commanders in that operation was Naletilic, Tuta. Moving on, touch very briefly in some of the time remaining before the first recess, moving to the attack on the Vranica building on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, as I said earlier only a few weeks later. And I submit to the Chamber that given the volume of evidence that the Chamber has received, it is sometimes easy, or has been for me, to forget the connection of some of these events or their proximity in time. The attack on the Vranica building on the 9th and 10th of May is only days after Sovici-Doljani, only days. In fact, one might say the bodies in Sovici-Doljani weren't even cold yet. And here was Tuta again at the forefront of the HVO charge, attacking the Vranica building in Mostar. Now, I don't think we should minimise the importance of the Vranica building from a symbolic perspective. The evidence showed that at the end of the day there was only a small group of soldiers there, probably no than 20, maybe 30. Did it really constitute much armed resistance to the more HVO? No. But it symbolised the organised, armed Muslim resistance, or at least potential resistance in West Mostar. And the pattern that the Chamber will see over and over again in the evidence is in the ethnic cleansing that occurred whether it was in Sovici or the Vranica building or in Rastani or elsewhere is that the first thing you do is take care of the military-age men and the armed resistance. And once they are under control, you deal with the rest of the population at your leisure. Because then the Muslim women and children, the elderly can be taken care of without much trouble really. And it was Naletilic that did it. On the 9th of May and again the evidence could be discussed at much greater length and is in our brief, but there has been much discussion about what happened and who started the attack on the 9th of May. Let me make two submissions to the Chamber. First of all, it is the Prosecution's view respectfully based on the weight of the evidence, on the overwhelming weight of the evidence, that the HVO attacked Mostar, specifically West Mostar, at approximately 5.00 in the morning on the 9th of May, 1993. Having said that, let me just indicate to the Chamber, whether that's true or not really has no bearing on the charges. Whoever started it, whoever pulled the trigger first, has nothing to do, does not absolve for a moment the mass arrest of Muslim civilians that were taken out of their flats, that were taken to Velez stadium, that were put on buses that day and taken to the Heliodrom. It does not absolve for a moment the Muslim men who were taken out of the Vranica building, taken to the tobacco institute, presented to Tuta, and personally mistreated by Tuta himself and his subordinates. Who fired the first shot really doesn't matter at all. Now, having said that, again Sir Martin Garrod told us that this was clearly a preplanned, deliberate attack. You remember that Sir Martin was the former commanding officer -- not one commanding officer, the commanding officer of the British Royal Marines, a professional soldier all his life. And he told the Chamber what it would take to organise a military operation on this scale. You don't do it on five minute's notice. You don't do it in a reaction to some Muslim insult on a street in West Mostar. This was planned, logistics had to be put in place, the buses had to be arranged, the collection centres had to be designated at the Velez stadium and elsewhere. This was a preplanned, concerted orchestrated attack that took days to organise. That's what the military professional soldier, Sir Martin, told you, and others. Tuta was there. Two indications of that in addition to other evidence are the fact that Juka Prazina was there and played a key role repeatedly identified by witnesses and one of Tuta's other deputies, Zeljko Bosnjak played a key role and was there. In fact, on Exhibit 17.2, it's a videotape, the Chamber will recall a videotape of the men coming out of the Vranica building and then some other clips as well. In the middle of that clip, Zeljko Bosnjak is interviewed, interviewed that day, and who is he but one of the lead deputy commanders, along with Prazina of the Convicts Battalion. And Exhibit 17.3, I don't know if you have that, Mr. Bos, but is a still simply a still photo made from the videotape and there is Bosnjak. There he is at the Vranica building on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993. In fact, before I leave the Vranica building, one of the Defence's own witness, another relatively experienced military man, Witness NP, not a Prosecution witness, Mr. President, a Defence witness, Witness NP saw Juka taking prisoners to the Ministry of Defence building. He saw Juka arguing with a prisoner. He saw Tuta at the Ministry of Defence on the 10th of May. He saw the yard at the tobacco institute awash with people, civilians, and soldiers. He saw -- or, in fact, Tuta spoke with the Defence Witness NP and some of the soldiers from his unit. All put Tuta there, in addition to the extensive Prosecution witness testimony that put him there. Couple of brief points. It is the Prosecution's view and the Prosecution case, Mr. President, Your Honours, that the man Naletilic Tuta has what we call the 7(3) command responsibility not only concerning the Vinko Skrobo ATG, but for the conduct of the other ATGs that were part of the Convicts Battalion and over which he was superior. The Chamber heard about the Benko Penavic ATG, the Baja Kraljevic ATG, other ATGs. The Prosecution case was confirmed unexpectedly, was not an exhibit at the beginning of the case, but was confirmed to the letter -- to the letter, in the Karlo Rotim book a part of which is Exhibit P927/2 describing in detail the structure of the Convicts Battalion, of Tuta being its commander, and of the ATGs that were part of it, including the Vinko Skrobo, commanded by Vinko Martinovic, the Baja Kraljevic commanded by Predrag Mandic, the Benko Penavic commanded by Mario Milicevic, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. Very quickly, if Mr. Bos has Exhibits P51 and P52 if he could put those on the ELMO. Small pieces, Your Honour, but part of the hundreds of exhibits that the Prosecution has given to you. If these units were not part of the Convicts Battalion, if they were not Tuta's units, then why do their patch say, Kaznjenicka Bojna, on the patch? And the exhibit, the first one for the Vinko Skrobo and the second one for the Baja Kraljevic ATG. There is extensive evidence in our brief, those are just samples. Secondly, Your Honour, the second point that we would make is that in terms as a commander, Naletilic was responsible for the care of prisoners taken by his troops. It was not sufficient -- it was not allowable for Tuta time after time, whether in Sovici-Doljani or at the Vranica building or elsewhere to take prisoners and then simply forget about them. He as a commander has responsibility to see the prisoners are treated according to the laws of international humanitarian law, according to the Geneva Conventions. He simply cannot wash his hands and go on about his business. Mr. President, that is a brief overview of the Prosecution case. As I said at the beginning, could not cover it in any detail. There was -- there is also the attack on Rastani. It's in our brief. There are other aspects of the Prosecution case which are covered in our brief. Of course, Mr. Stringer now will turn his attention after the break to the case concerning Mr. Martinovic. And then I look forward to addressing the Chamber again at the end of the day. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, shall we have the break now? We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May it please the Court, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel for the Defence, like Mr. Scott, I will not engage in any sort of wholesale restatement of the evidence, certainly it's all found -- everything that we have to say about the evidence is found in the brief. I intend to use the time allotted to me to discuss the crimes and criminal responsibility of Vinko Martinovic in this case and will use this occasion to respond to a variety of the assertions he and his defence have made in their final submissions, their brief. I will then also briefly address the proof of Croatia's direct military participation in this conflict, which is one of the bases on which the Prosecution submits that it has proven the existence of an international armed conflict in this case. Mr. President, my first comments would be of a general nature, some general observations about the application of article 7 in this case in respect of Vinko Martinovic. The Trial Chamber will find, if it hasn't already, that the Defence devotes a significant amount of discussion in its brief to article 7(3) under the Statute, asserting that Mr. Martinovic cannot be held responsible under article 7(3) for a variety of reasons, claiming that he was not a military commander, that he acted in the capacity of a civilian commander, for example, that he didn't know of crimes committed by subordinates, et cetera. The Prosecution rejects these assertions because it's our submission, Mr. President, they are not supported by the evidence or by the law. Mr. Martinovic's military authority as a commander, a military commander in this case, is in our view beyond doubt. He was not a civilian. He did not wield authority as a civilian. He was at all times a military commander in a position to exercise responsible command over subordinates in his unit. The evidence I think amply demonstrates in fact the manner in which Mr. Martinovic in fact exercised his authority and his control over his subordinates. Throughout the trial, the Defence has in fact never asserted that Martinovic could not or did not have the ability to exercise command and effective control over his subordinates. The fact that this unit held and successfully defended a strategic section of the confrontation line at the Bulevar in Mostar is itself proof that Martinovic exercised command and control over his subordinates. Mr. President, the main point that I wish to emphasise on -- in respect of article 7 is that the Defence submissions in respect of article 7(3) must not distract the Trial Chamber from the primary basis of Martinovic's criminal responsibility, which is found under Article 7(1). Martinovic ordered crimes. He planned crimes. He personally committed crimes. And in doing so, he instigated crimes, the many crimes, committed by his subordinates. Martinovic regularly called upon his subordinates to commit and participate in crimes directed against Muslim prisoners in the confrontation line, at his headquarters, near the confrontation line, and against those many civilian residents of West Mostar whom he and his subordinates forcibly evicted and transferred across into East Mostar. For Vinko Martinovic, this is first and foremost a case of criminal responsibility under Article 7(1). In their brief, the Defence ignore Article 7(1) entirely. Their response to the overwhelming proof of Martinovic's personal involvement and guilt for the crimes charged is simply to assert that the witnesses called were not credible and to make their oft-repeated and never-proved claims about the AID. I am not going to devote any time during this argument debating or assessing for the Trial Chamber, if you will, the credibility of the witnesses who came, the many witnesses who came and testified about the events in which they participated, the things that happened to them. The Trial Chamber certainly is in the best position to judge the credibility of all the witnesses that it's heard in this case. But because of the strength of the Prosecution case proving Martinovic's guilt and direct responsibility for all the crimes with which he's charged in the indictment under Article 7(1), we point out that the Trial Chamber may in fact never even need to consider the Defence submissions on article 7(3). Having said that, Mr. President, there is there is one vital aspect of the law of command responsibility which has been totally ignored by the Defence in their submissions which the Trial Chamber may find useful in its consideration of Martinovic's conduct and omissions in respect of prisoners who found themselves in his custody. Mr. Scott touched upon this briefly in his remarks, and that is the fact that under international humanitarian law, every commander has an obligation, an affirmative obligation, to ensure that prisoners in their custody, prisoners in their charge, are treated humanely in accordance with international law. It's incumbent upon military commanders such as Vinko Martinovic to ensure that procedures, practices, are in place to ensure that the rights of prisoners of war, civilians as well, are honoured at all times when those prisoners are in his custody or in the custody of his subordinates. That obligation was reaffirmed, I believe, most recently in the Blaskic Trial Chamber decision after having considered a number of the post World War II cases. This was Martinovic's obligation in respect of all prisoners for whom he took responsibility. He cannot, as he suggests in his brief, attempt to lay off responsibility for prisoners to those people who were out at the Heliodrom, the administrators or the military police who had custody of prisoners when they were at the Heliodrom. The prisoners' entitlement to proper and humane treatment followed them from the Heliodrom to Vinko Martinovic's headquarters on the Kalemova Street in West Mostar. He's responsible for everything that happened to those prisoners when they were brought to work for him and his unit. I'm speaking of all of the prisoners who were brought to the ATG Vinko Skrobo, who were forced to work in the confrontation line, on the Bulevar making sandbags, moving sandbags, digging fortifications and trenches. I'm talking about the prisoners who died on the 17th of September, 1993, during the military operations that occurred on that day, and I'm also speaking of Nenad Haramandic, a prisoner who as the parties now appear to agree was in fact at the headquarters of Vinko Skrobo and was brought to Vinko Martinovic on the day in question. I'll talk about that all in a few moments. In respect of counts 2 through 8, Mr. President, which are the group of counts that relate to forced labour of prisoners, detainees, on the confrontation line, the evidence establishes that Martinovic and the ATG Vinko Skrobo participated virtually every day in an organised, highly regulated, highly documented, system within the HVO for using Muslim prisoners to perform unlawful labour in dangerous confrontation line positions. In respect of the ATG Vinko Skrobo, the Trial Chamber has heard the testimony of numerous witnesses who were themselves brought from the Heliodrom and forced to perform any number of acts placing themselves at risk routinely and regularly in what can only be described as an incredibly brutal confrontation line that existed across the Bulevar in West Mostar. The Trial Chamber heard not only from victim witnesses, the Trial Chamber heard testimony about this practice from members of Mr. Martinovic's own unit. I refer to Allan Knudsen and Witness Q, and I also refer to the testimony of Witness S who was a member of the HVO 4th battalion who was ordered and given responsibility to guard prisoners who were in the custody of Vinko Martinovic and were forced to work in his area of responsibility. I'm going to ask Mr. Bos to quickly place Exhibit 562.2 on the ELMO. This is one of the many reports which the Trial Chamber has documenting the removal and the return of prisoners to and from the Heliodrom for work with the many, many HVO units in Mostar, and HV units, I might add - and I'll get to that later - which used prisoners for unlawful labour. We know, and the Trial Chamber recalls, I'm sure, the great deal of testimony regarding Dinko Kenezovic, who was often charged with going to the Heliodrom and bringing the prisoners back from the Heliodrom to work for Vinko Martinovic and his unit. This particular report memorialises the wounding of one of the prisoners that had been released to Mr. Martinovic's unit in August of 1993. The bottom of the report appears the signature of Stanko Bozic who wrote many reports about the conditions at the Heliodrom and the mistreatment of prisoners who were taken for forced labour. The Trial Chamber will also recall the extensive HVO logbooks which are in evidence which provide a great deal of documentation concerning the dates, the numbers, and the identities of witnesses who were taken out of the Heliodrom to perform forced labour. The fact is, Mr. President, that this accused, Vinko Martinovic, and his unit routinely and regularly used prisoners unlawfully to perform extremely, highly dangerous tasks in an active confrontation line, tasks which he deemed too dangerous for himself or his own subordinates to perform. One last question the Trial Chamber may wish to ask itself when it considers this group of counts in the indictment - and I may ask this question again in my remarks concerning the other facts of the case, and other counts - we know the extent to which this practice occurred among the HVO, all units, during the entire time of this conflict, certainly after the events of 30 June, 1993. Knowing what the Trial Chamber knows about Vinko Martinovic, knowing what the Trial Chamber knows about the conduct of his subordinates, is it the least bit reasonable to question whether he would have in fact used prisoners to perform these tasks rather than using his own subordinates? Is it reasonable to conclude that he would not have permitted prisoners to be used for these purposes? Is there any evidence to suggest that he attempted to prevent these sorts of activities, this unlawful conduct, from taking place within his own, as the Defence would assert, very small area of responsibility? Mr. President, it's our submission that in fact the evidence does not permit any conclusion that he would have taken any measures to prevent this conduct, and that he knew this conduct was taking place, actively promoted it and now in our view, Mr. President, finds himself having been proven to be guilty of the crimes associated with the unlawful use of forced labour. The events of 17 September, I will briefly address. The Trial Chamber knows a great deal about that day. We know that there was a major HVO operation that took place in Mostar on that day, an attack was launched along the entire length of the confrontation line, along the Bulevar, in Mr. Martinovic's area of responsibility, all the way down north to the area of Santiceva Street. The Trial Chamber only recently heard the testimony of Witness AF, whose brother was killed on Santiceva Street on that day. Witness AF was then involved in the burial of a hundred or so bodies of Muslim prisoners who were killed in the operation on the 17th of September. We know that on that day, a special group of prisoners, a different group of prisoners, was brought from the Heliodrom to Vinko Martinovic. Much of the planning that went into the operation of 17 September, 1993, is contained in Exhibit P608. Mr. Bos has that, if we could take a quick look. I should first point out, Mr. President, that in their brief, it appears to me that the Defence concede the correctness or the reliability of this document, 608. The Defence for Mr. Martinovic assert that the document in fact establishes that the events of 17 September, 1993, fell under the command of Mario Milicevic and that therefore, Mr. Martinovic could bear no criminal or command responsibility for the acts of 17 September, 1993. We disagree with that submission, Mr. President. We submit that the evidence establishes conclusively that Mr. Martinovic was actively involved in the planning and directing of certainly the actions of the ATG Vinko Skrobo on the 17th of September, 1993. Referring to Exhibit 608, particularly on the second page, we find and we will find this time and time again when we examine the documents regarding the activities of Mr. Martinovic, that in fact his activities and the activities of 17 September are linked to his superior, Mr. Mladen Naletilic. The second paragraph of page 2, in fact, refers to a meeting called by Mr. Naletilic in which he summoned his commanders of his ATG groups, or at least three of them, to Siroki Brijeg for meetings with others to engage in the planning of the operation on 17 September, 1993. We know that Tuta's men were involved in this operation. We know that Vinko Martinovic was involved in this operation. The third and final page of this document provides additional corroboration concerning a lot of the witness -- victim-witness testimony regarding the events of the 17th of September in which it states that the attack began at exactly 1200 hours, 12 noon, on the 17th. The Trial Chamber heard testimony from several witnesses, and has before it the testimony of several witnesses, on that point. We know that on the 17th of September, 1993, a group of prisoners was signed out of the Heliodrom by Dinko Kenezovic and taken to the headquarters of the ATG Vinko Skrobo, that is shown in a couple of pages that are found in one of the log books, Exhibit P601.1. Mr. President, this is a part of the logbook for the 17th of September, 1993. It shows the names of those prisoners who were taken to Vinko Martinovic on this day. It includes the name of prisoners who died on the confrontation line on this day. We know that the wooden rifles incident in particular was planned ahead of time. We know because first of all it was necessary to make the wooden rifles. We also know it was planned because as Witness I testified, that's a day when the usual group of prisoners was not taken to Mr. Martinovic. We've heard a lot in the Defence submissions about the favoured group of prisoners, the prisoners that perhaps knew him or the prisoners who perhaps possessed certain skills which Mr. Martinovic needed, particularly in repairing the many cars at his disposal. But on this day, the usual group of prisoners got up to go with Mr. Kenezovic and were told that they weren't needed. A different group of prisoners was taken and that's the group whose name appears on the logbook that is in Exhibit P601.1. We know that the prisoners were given wooden rifles. We know that Vinko Martinovic was directly involved in selecting and equipping the prisoners with camouflage uniforms and the wooden rifles. That he was directly involved instructing them on their mission. We know that the mission took place at 12 noon when other prisoners were instructed to remove sandbags from the area of Liska Street so that the tank could pass through, passing closer toward the ABiH positions on the other side. We have not only the testimony of victim witnesses who participated in these events. We also have the testimony of two of the members of Mr. Martinovic's unit, Allan Knudsen and Witness Q who testified about their own participation in these events and the participation of the prisoners in the carrying of the wooden rifles in front of the tank. The Defence in their brief rely on Exhibit P612.1, which is a document purporting to indicate that all of the prisoners signed out on this day, the 17th, in fact returned to the Heliodrom. Mr. President, we know that that document is wrong; it is false. In fact, not all of the prisoners signed out to Mr. Martinovic on that day did return to the Heliodrom. We know that at least two of them, and probably three of them, were killed in the area of the Bulevar confrontation line on the 17th of September, and I'm going to briefly turn to two of those prisoners, Aziz Colakovic and Enes Pajo. The Trial Chamber will find their names appearing among those who were signed out to Vinko Martinovic on the 17th of September. We know that these two prisoners were performing forced labour in the active, dangerous area of the confrontation line during the HVO operation on the 17th of September. Witness I was with Aziz Colakvic on that day. They were both at the sandbag barrier on Liska Street. They had been given a number of tasks to perform by Ernest Takac, the very well-known and notorious subordinate and colleague of Mr. Martinovic. Witness I and Aziz Colakvic were subsequently separated by events. Later, Witness I was with Hamdija Colakvic inside the health centre when they were instructed to remove sandbags from the windows. Later, Takac instructed Witness I to move north to an area above the health centre, to remove the body of a wounded HVO soldier who was out in an open area on the confrontation line. In moving to this area, in order to get to this soldier, Witness I found and saw the dead body of Aziz Colakvic in a clearing, and in fact at that point, Witness I was himself hit by a bullet in the leg and found himself hiding behind the body of his friend, Aziz Colakvic in the middle of this battle on the Bulevar. The same day, Witness NN recognised the body of Enes Pajo lying in a pool of blood after Witness NN had been told, ordered, to get out of the trench and to remove wounded and dead bodies from this area. We know from Witness J that Enes Pajo was in fact one of the prisoners who had initially been selected to carry one of the wooden rifles by Vinko Martinovic earlier that morning. Mr. President, the documents and the testimony establish that these two prisoners were among those taken to Mr. Vinko Martinovic on the 17th of September. The evidence establishes beyond any doubt that these prisoners were among all of the others who were deliberately forced to work in an area in which there was an extremely high likelihood of death or serious injury. It's true, we don't know whether these two died as a result of being used as human shields, but it's our submission, Mr. President, that we do know that Vinko Martinovic bears individual criminal responsibility for the deaths of those two prisoners on the Bulevar confrontation line on that day. Counts 13 through 17 relate to the beating and death of Nenad Harmandic. I'm not going to go into great detail over the extensive evidence, the detailed evidence that has been submitted in respect of this issue. I will use this occasion to respond and to address some of the points and assertions made by the Defence in their case and in their final trial brief. Mr. President, it seems that after -- at the end of this long trial, we do have agreement on at least a couple of very critical facts relating to Nenad Harmandic. Agreement, that is, with the Defence of Mr. Martinovic. We know and the Defence of Mr. Martinovic appears to concede, that in fact Nenad Harmandic was brought to Vinko Martinovic and the headquarters of the ATG Vinko Skrobo. I'm referring to paragraph 351 of the Defence brief. The Defence also agree or concede that when he was at the headquarters of the Vinko Skrobo, Mr. Harmandic was in a state of having been severely beaten. Both of these points corroborate and are consistent with the testimony of Prosecution witnesses, Halil Ajanic and Witness AD, who testified that she saw Mr. Harmandic at Martinovic's headquarters. We know based on the testimony of Halil Ajanic, the severe beating that was inflicted on Mr. Harmandic at Mr. Martinovic's headquarters by Mr. Martinovic's subordinates, Ernest Takac in particular. We know that Vinko Martinovic invited Halil Ajanic, himself a prisoner, to participate in this severe beating that was taking place. The Trial Chamber has already heard Mr. Ajanic's testimony about other forms of outrage, outrageous conduct and acts that were directed against Mr. Harmandic before he was finally put in a car by Mr. Martinovic's subordinates and taken away. And it's conceded, Mr. President, that that's the last we know about what happened to Mr. Harmandic. The Defence offer two explanations or defences in respect of Nenad Harmandic which are perhaps related. First is their assertion that Mr. Harmandic had been severely beaten at the Heliodrom and that he was then brought in that condition to Mr. Martinovic, who saw him and simply sent him back to the Heliodrom. The Defence also point to a couple of documents in evidence. One is Exhibit P774, which indicates that in fact Mr. Harmandic was signed out in mid-July, 1993, not by the ATG Vinko Skrobo but instead by the 1st HVO military police light assault Battalion. The Defence assert that Mr. Harmandic was in their custody and control and that whatever happened to him was not the responsibility of Mr. Martinovic. And that in fact this particular document indicates that Mr. Harmandic had managed to escape. Mr. President, it's our submission that there is no evidence or logic that supports the assertion that Harmandic would have been brought to the ATG Vinko Skrobo headquarters from the Heliodrom if he had already been severely beaten there by others. Nor does that rule out the likelihood that any such beatings would have continued upon Mr. Harmandic's arrival at the ATG Vinko Skrobo. In any event, it's our submission that it makes no sense to bring a prisoner to the front line who can't work, because we know that the prisoners brought to Mr. Martinovic's headquarters were brought there to work. It's equally implausible, Mr. President, that Vinko Martinovic would have sent Harmandic back to the Heliodrom after the severe beating that was inflicted on Harmandic at that headquarters. The orders with which prisoners were released to all of the units, including the Vinko Skrobo unit, required and reminded the commanders that the prisoners were to be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. We know that Mr. Stanko Bozic, the warden at the Heliodrom prison, was regularly writing reports about the mistreatment that prisoners were suffering when they were in the custody of individual HVO units. To return Harmandic to the Heliodrom would have been to reveal to everyone, both the prisoners and the HVO military personnel at the Heliodrom, the treatment that Harmandic received while he was in Martinovic's custody. Martinovic had no choice but to ensure that Harmandic's condition was kept secret. The fact is, Mr. President, it was easier and safer for Martinovic to have Harmandic killed or to kill him, himself, rather than to allow him to be returned to the Heliodrom in the condition of near death. He therefore told the prisoners - and the Trial Chamber heard testimony about this - that Harmandic would not be returning with them to the Heliodrom on that day, and that he had tried to escape. That lie is in fact reflected in the documentation in respect of this incident. On the ELMO, Exhibit P774, in which Martinovic's lie about what really happened to Harmandic is reflected in the paperwork in order to cover up what really happened. Mr. President, this exhibit, 774, is useful for another reason which, in our submission, strongly corroborates the testimony of Halil Ajanic. When it reviews the testimony of Mr. Ajanic, the Trial Chamber will find that Mr. Ajanic in fact recalled that the persons who removed Harmandic from the Heliodrom on that day were the so-called Strump brothers. He said the sons of Ivan Culo. We find on Exhibit P774, that in fact Harmandic appears to have been signed out or the responsible person for his release was in fact someone named mill Yenko Culo. It's our submission, Mr. President, that Ajanic accurately recalled for the Trial Chamber not only the identity of the persons who removed Harmandic from the Heliodrom and took him to Vinko Martinovic, but that this small detail, this important detail, should tell the Trial Chamber much more about the credibility and reliability of Mr. Ajanic's testimony about this entire incident. We know from the testimony of Witness AF that it was routine, that it was certainly not unusual, for prisoners to be signed out of the Heliodrom by representative of the military police and taken to Vinko Martinovic. The fact that Harmandic was or may have been signed out of the Heliodrom by Miljenko Culo does not mean that he could not have gone to the headquarters of Vinko Martinovic. What it does mean, Mr. President, we submit, is that Mr. Ajanic, to this day, has a clear recollection of all the events that he testified about in relation to Mr. Harmandic. Mr. President, count 18 charges Mr. Martinovic with forcible transfer of civilians from West Mostar during the months following the HVO attack of 9 May, 1993. While the forced labour counts in the indictment provide the Trial Chamber with insight into the harsh treatment that Martinovic inflicted on Muslim male detainees who were held at the Heliodrom, the evidence proving count 18 reveals the brutality with which Martinovic and his subordinates set upon those defenceless Muslim women, children, and elderly, who remained behind in their homes and their flats in West Mostar, living in fear of the night when the armed HVO soldiers who arrive at their door and drive them across the Neretva river into the hell that awaited them on the east side. The evidence indicates that this form of ethnic cleansing took place regularly in the months following the outbreak of the conflict, with expelled civilians sometimes crossing into East Mostar in small groups, and at other times in huge waves. We know that during that time, the population living in East Mostar, under the burden of siege, daily indiscriminate shelling, and sniping swelled from some 25.000 to approximately 55.000. The Prosecution submits that before the Trial Chamber in this case is one of the leading perpetrators of this form of ethnic cleansing, Vinko Martinovic. Mr. President, I'm going to at this point refer the Trial Chamber to our brief in which we have - it's our submission - very carefully and comprehensively addressed two of the waves of ethnic cleansing that occurred in West Mostar, based both on the witness testimony and the documents in evidence. One of these is the expulsions that occurred on the 13th and 14th of June, 1993. These expulsions are documented in a number of exhibits, including Exhibit P452.1, which is the note received by ECMM monitor Van der Grinten in which he was informed of the names of the HVO personnel who were responsible for this round of ethnic cleansing. Mr. President, that exhibit is on the ELMO; that's the original. You can see, I believe, the very faded typewritten names which appear there, which are in fact the names Vinko Martinovic, Ernest Takac, and Nino Pehar. This information is corroborated by information contained in other documents in evidence, and I'm going to skip one document and I'm going to go directly to P456.2. Mr. President, the HVO's own documents confirmed memorialised this round of ethnic cleansing from the Dum neighbourhood of Mostar on the 13th and 14th of June. Exhibit 456.2 is a military police report of the HVO 1st Battalion. I bring this particular report to the Trial Chamber's attention in response to testimony and assertions made by the Defence about the alleged practice in which other soldiers, other bad people, doing bad things would falsely invoke the name of Vinko Martinovic while they were carrying out these crimes. The fact is, Mr. President, as these documents demonstrate, Vinko Martinovic was himself identified as being on the scene leading this operation. This wasn't other soldiers claiming to be him. He was there. He was personally identified as taking part in this ethnic cleansing operation. It's worth also noting, Mr. President, as indicated in this report, that when asked by the military police what these soldiers were doing, they said that they had been ordered by Tuta to take the Muslims and to drive them out of this section and send them to the other side. Mr. President, it's no coincidence that yet again we see the HVO's own documentation linking Martinovic and his crimes to those of his commander, Mladen Naletilic. Mr. President, it's our submission that the Trial Chamber has every reason, every justification, to fully rely on all of the evidence that's been submitted in respect of this round of ethnic cleansings from mid-June 1993 in which Mr. Martinovic directly participated on behalf of his commander, Mr. Naletilic. The second round, wave, of expulsions that occurred occurred on the 29th of September, 1993, in the Centar II neighbourhood of West Mostar. And on this point, Mr. President, I'd ask if we could briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Exhibit 620.1 is an HVO, SIS report of 1 October, 1993. It memorialises the events and the wave of ethnic cleansing that occurred on the night of the 29th. Once again, this document links Vinko Martinovic to this wave of ethnic cleansing that occurred, not only as a participant but as an organiser, a planner, and a commander. We know that this document confirms in several important respects the testimony that I just referred to in private session. The reference to the persons - referring now to the first paragraph on the second page - who were separated into different categories and sent to the left bank near the health centre, and also in the next paragraph, the testimony about the cries that could be heard coming from the buildings across from the dairy store. That's another location the Trial Chamber heard about in that testimony. And once again, Mr. President, in the final paragraph of this document, we find a reference linking this particular ethnic cleansing operation to Mr. Martinovic's co-accused, Mr. Naletilic, based on the fact that Colonel Ivan Andabak was one of the individuals whom this incident was reported to. Mr. President, I need to -- if I could go back into private session again just for one very brief moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President the Trial Chamber may recall that in fact the events of 29 and 30 September, 1993, were captured on film by a BBC journalist named Jeremy Bowen who happened to be in East Mostar at the time making a documentary. With your permission, Mr. President, I'd like to play just a few short minutes from that videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: VOICE OF JEREMY BOWEN: "A few yards away, the operation on Medina was still going on. They had time to do the best they could for her, no other casualties had come in. It gets no better at night. 500 Muslims had just been robbed and thrown out of their homes in West Mostar by the Croats. They had to cross the River Neretva to get to comparative safety on a bridge made of ropes and planks. Bosnian soldiers told them which way to go. The Croats were shooting at the people they just made refugees. Only a few hours before, until the Croat gangs had come for them and forced them over the front line, they thought that they were safe. They had been settling down for the night. The Croat machine-guns didn't let up and the refugees kept on coming. They were trying to kill old men and women, mothers and their children. She was so frightened she could barely walk, but she tried to calm her sons. Each new family has to be fed and housed. This is a war crime with a cold purpose: To increase the pressure on the military authorities in East Mostar, the brutality of the expulsions drives home the message that compromise with Croat extremists is neither possible nor desirable. The refugees spent their first night in East Mostar in a bombed-out theatre. In one evening, all of them had lot their homes and possessions. They talked of persecution, rape, and murder."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, the evidence establishes the documents that relate to this expulsion. The testimony in closed session which I referred to a few moments ago relate to this round of expulsions. Jeremy Bowen testified that this footage was in fact taken on the night of the 29th of September, 1993. Mr. President, the Trial Chamber, we submit, has evidence before it that proves conclusively that this accused, Vinko Martinovic, was in fact the person on the other side of the river that night. He was the person, he was the reason why all of these Muslims were forced to cross that river, those women, those old people, those children, were forced to cross that foot bridge in the middle of the night and spend their first night as refugees in a bombed-out old movie theatre East Mostar. In his brief at paragraph 246, Mr. Martinovic makes this claim: "It cannot be said that in those situations there were expulsions and forcible transfers of the population, but those were voluntary transfers caused by war circumstances. The greatest part of the population moved in that way, and it is impermissible to ignore that and charge Vinko Martinovic and his unit." Mr. President, if the Trial Chamber concludes that what it just saw, and if it concludes that the testimony of the many witnesses who testified about their experience during these forced evictions was in fact a voluntary transfer, then we should let Mr. Martinovic return to Mostar. The fact is the evidence compels a contrary finding by this Trial Chamber. Mr. President, it's our submission that in fact Mr. Martinovic bears a high degree of responsibility for the many hundreds of forced evictions, brutal acts, brutal violence committed against the Muslim population of West Mostar during the course of the conflict against the ABiH. One last few remarks about discriminatory intent and this relates to the persecution charged in count 1. In paragraph 152 of their brief, Mr. Martinovic claims that he did not possess the requisite mens rea for persecution. He didn't possess intent to discriminate against Muslims. In support of that, he cites the testimony of a group of Muslim persons that he called to testify on his behalf who were apparently protected by him in one way or another during the conflict. We don't know the reasons why Mr. Martinovic may have decided to assist a small number of Muslims, to shield them from the brutality that he and his comrades were visiting on large numbers of less fortunate Muslims throughout West Mostar. One Defence witness in fact said that every Croat in West Mostar had his Muslim, one or more of them, that they protected. Likewise, on the east side, Muslims had one or more Croats that they protected. There were indications that Mr. Martinovic protected those who were friends of his family or those with whom he had fought in his HOS unit against the Serbs in 1992. Whatever the reasons why Mr. Martinovic may have decided to assist a small number of these Muslims whom he favoured, we certainly know that there were hundreds of other Muslims who did not find themselves in his favour. Those few Muslims whom he produced in the courtroom were not his victims. His victims, either those compelled to work in the confrontation line and in his area of responsibility, or those defenseless civilians whom he expelled into East Mostar, those were his victims, and those were exclusively Muslim. We know that Vinko Martinovic and his subordinates often used the derogatory term "balija" when they were shouting at the Muslims during the course of expulsions or shouting out orders for forced labour. It's our submission, Mr. President, that Mr. Martinovic did in fact act and possess a high degree of discriminatory intent as part of his contribution to the overall HVO campaign to cleanse the Muslims from Mostar. Our position on this point or this defence, if you will, was very eloquently set forth in one of the international military Tribunal cases from post World War II in Nuremberg, the U.S. versus von Weizsaecker, the so-called ministry's case.
