With your permission, Mr. President, I'd like to just read a very short passage from this trial which very, as I said, eloquently sets forth our position on this. "We reject the claim that good intentions render innocent that which is otherwise criminal, and which asserts that one may with impunity commit serious crimes because he hopes thereby to prevent others or that general benevolence towards individuals is a cloak or justification for participation in crimes against the unknown many." Mr. President, in this trial, in respect of Vinko Martinovic, we concern ourselves with the crimes committed in Mostar against the unknown many, not the favoured few who escaped persecution and worse, because of the whim or the fancy of Vinko Martinovic. It's our submission, Mr. President, that the evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt Vinko Martinovic acted with discriminatory intent, in fact hatred, intentionally targeting his victims because they were Muslims as part of his part in the overall campaign against the Muslims of Mostar. Mr. President, I'm going to move on now to a separate subject, a different subject. Perhaps I can even finish before the break, and that is the subject of Croatia's participation in this conflict. The Croatian -- the participation of the Republic of Croatia in respect of the conflict involved in this case, that is the HVO-ABiH conflict that began at the very latest in 1993, probably in 1992, the participation extended to a number of levels. Our overall submission on this, Mr. President, and Mr. Scott I'm sure is going to say this again when he comes back after the break with his remarks, Croatia's direct participation in this conflict, the deployment of HV generals, high ranking officers, HV units, into Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of this conflict is merely an extension or a consequence, a natural consequence, of the overall policy of Croatia and its president at that time, Franjo Tudjman, in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly those parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina that fell within the territory of the so-called Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. This policy and this conduct extends in fact earlier quite a bit earlier, than many of the events that the Trial Chamber has heard about in this case. I would like to very quickly run through a series of exhibits which the Trial Chamber may not yet be familiar with, which in our submission very graphically demonstrates the effect and the participation of Croatian military personnel, high ranking military personnel, in the conflict and the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina going back to April of 1992. And I'm going to start with Exhibit 122.1, just to set the facts for the Trial Chamber. Mr. President, this goes back to the very beginning of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was on the 8th of April, 1992, when Bosnian president, Alija Izetbegovic, issued this order, this regulation. What he did was to cancel the previous Territorial Defence, TO, of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to establish a new one. This was essentially an establishment of an armed forces for the newly established, newly proclaimed, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The next exhibit is 122. On the very same day, Mate Boban, on behalf of the HZ HB, in fact signed a decision on the creation of a parallel, separate militia, also in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that of the HVO. The HVO was established on the same day as the TO. Two days later -- the next document is 123, two days later, we start to see the extent to which Mate Boban and the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna intend to cooperate with the TO in the joint defence against the Serbs that we've heard so much about from the Defence. This is the 10th of April, 1992. Two days -- sorry, two months before the liberation of Mostar, very early time in the conflict. Drawing the Trial Chamber's attention to the bottom third of the document, the Croatian Defence Council will have exclusive Supreme Command of these forces. This body is the only legal one. And its name is the only official one. Moving down, "As of today, 10 April, the main headquarters of the HVO will communicate solely with municipal headquarters of the HVO. All other military formations on the territory of Herceg-Bosna are either illegal or enemy formations. All other titles are no longer in official use." That's on the 10th of April, 1992. Mr. President, what I'm going to quickly do now is move down the chain of command so the Trial Chamber can see precisely how this order was implemented on the ground by HVO units acting under the orders and commands of an active major general of the Croatian Army. Exhibit P127 is an order issued on the 8th of May, 1992, by Colonel General Ante Roso. Roso is clearly taking the order, the previous order, from Boban and then moving it down the chain of command, declaring that the only legal military units in the territory of the HZ HB are units of the HVO. Item 5: This order supersedes all orders of the Territorial Defence command which shall be considered illegal in this territory. This territory being Herceg-Bosna. Now, the next exhibit is 654.3. We are moving ahead about a year and a half now to October 1993. Ante Roso, the person who issued this order in May of 1992, outlawing the TO on behalf of the HVO main staff was himself a general in the Croatian Army in May of 1992 and at all times thereafter, until he resigned from the Croatian Army in October of 1993, as shown in 654.3. Roso only resigned from the Croatian Army shortly before he was appointed to take command of the HVO main staff, replacing Slobodan Praljak in November of 1993. Next exhibit is 130. Roso's order, the order of a Colonel General of the Croatian Army issued in May of 1992 moved down the HVO chain of command. Three days later, on the 11th of May, 1992, Tihomir Blaskic, who was then the commander of the HVO operative zone based in Kiseljak, turned Roso's order around and in fact issued his own order implementing the Roso order, declaring that all orders of the TO are rendered invalid and the TO is in this area considered illegal. The next document is 128, 10th of May, 1992, Dario Kordic did the same thing in his area of responsibility, Busovaca. Item number 3, all paramilitary formations, the so-called TO, individuals and others, are given the ultimatum to hand over all weapons or to place themselves under HVO command, which includes the wearing of HVO insignia. Mr. President, the Trial Chamber heard evidence during the trial from a couple of witnesses, one of whom was a Defence expert witness, Mr. Marijan. Mr. Marijan testified about a series of armed conflicts between the HVO and the TO or the Armija that occurred during the spring of 1992. Mr. President, it's our submission that those armed conflicts between the TO and the HVO, going all the way back approximately a year before the first outright conflict charged as a crime in this case, April of 1993, those conflicts went all the way back to 1992, resulting from HVO attempts to implement Croatian Army General Roso's order to outlaw and disarm the TO in the territory of Herceg-Bosna. Now, the participation and the role of Croatia and its generals in the conflict against the Armija and the TO only intensified, but it finds its roots going back a year prior to the events of the highest relevance in this case, and in fact the Trial Chamber may wish to find, based on this evidence alone, that we had an international armed conflict between the HVO and the Armija going as far back as the spring of 1992, when you had an active HV general on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina outlawing orders -- issuing orders outlawing the Armija, the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We can take the break now, Mr. President, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you finished or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How long are you going to take?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will break here and we will resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to round off the subject of Ante Roso, the next exhibit is 664.2. As I mentioned just before the break, Mr. President, Mr. Roso only resigned from the Croatian Army in October of 1993, just prior to his appointment as chief of the HVO main staff, that is the HVO main staff. 664 is the document relating to that appointment. The Trial Chamber will note, going to the bottom first, that this is a document that appears over the name and title of Janko Bobetko, who was chief of the Croatian Army main staff, and also the name and title of Mr. Gojko Susak, who was at that time the Minister of Defence for the Republic of Croatia. This document is one in which Roso and a number of other HV personnel are appointed to positions within the main staff of the HVO down in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In addition to Roso, the Trial Chamber will note in item number 4, the name of Colonel Marijan Biskic, whose name and a number of documents which he authored figure prominently among the exhibits in evidence that relate to the abduction and disappearance of Robert Nosic from the HVO military police headquarters in Mostar following an operation against the military police that was led by Mr. Naletilic later during the month of November 1993. The predecessor of Ante Roso as chief of the HVO main staff was Slobodan Praljak who served in that capacity from July of 1993, until early November of 1993. The Trial Chamber may recall the testimony of Mr. Praljak when he testified in this case in which he agreed or conceded that he had commanded HVO units during operations in Prozor, Bosnia-Herzegovina, during October of 1992, and in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993. His testimony on that was that because of his position, because of the respect and the authority that he commanded, he was able in a de facto way to take command of HVO units. The point is for purposes of international armed conflict, Mr. President, that at the time he participated in those HVO operations in Prozor and Gornji Vakuf, he was in fact a general with the Croatian Army and in fact at the time he also held the position as assistant Minister of -- assistant to the Croatian Minister of Defence, Mr. Gojko Susak. This document, Exhibit 458.2, is one in which Praljak departs from the HV, resigns, if you will, from the HV, and then goes down to Bosnia-Herzegovina to take formal command over the HVO. We will see in a few moments that he then applied for reinstatement to the Croatian Army in the latter part of 1993 at the time of his departure from the HVO main staff. That is Exhibit 654.2. This is in fact a day or two before or after Ante Roso left the HV to take over the HVO. In this document, Mr. Praljak is applying to re-enter the HVO in advance of his departure from the HVO and then subsequent rejoining of the HV or Croatian Army after he was removed or resigned from his position as commander of the HVO main staff. Mr. President, the evidence establishes that these high level Croatian military personnel in fact moved seamlessly back and forth from the HV, Croatian Army, to the HVO. When they were in the HVO, when they were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the evidence establishes that these high level Croatian military personnel did in fact exercise command and control over HVO units under their command. Another document related to another officer from the HV, is Exhibit 559.1. Mr. President, in this document, we see that Major General Praljak, acting in his capacity as Chief of the Main Staff or as an HVO commander has sent this request to the Croatian Army, particularly to Mr. Susak as Minister of Defence, requesting the posting of HV officers to the HVO main staff. This particular document requests that Zarko Tole and Ivan Kapular be placed or posted in the HVO main staff. The Trial Chamber will find among the documents in evidence in this case a series of orders issued very shortly after the 4th of August, 1993, by Zarko Tole, who was then acting in his capacity as a member of the HVO main staff down in Mostar. We know that there were a number of other HV Croatian Army military personnel among the ranks of the HVO generally. That's indicated in two of the IAC documents that I briefly bring to the Trial Chamber's attention. One is IAC 35, an order dated 12th of April, 1993, signed by Zeljko Siljeg who was commander of the HVO northwest Herzegovina operative zone, in which he's requiring that all his personnel submit a list of all HV officers present in their units. A similar order is issued in IAC 36 on the same day by the commander of the HVO central Bosnia operative zone, Tihomir Blaskic, ordering submission of a list of all officers of the Croatian Army in his subordinate units. We know and the Trial Chamber has heard extensive testimony and has a number of documents in evidence which relate to the actual participation and presence of Croatian Army units in the Mostar region. Indeed, even at the Heliodrom, during the period of the conflict that the Trial Chamber has heard about in this case. Exhibit P638.2 is one of the many orders issued by Zlatan Mijo Jelic as commander of the Mostar Defence sector, permitting the release of prisoners to units of the HVO. In fact, this is one of Mr. Jelic's orders permitting the release of prisoners from the Heliodrom to an HV, Croatian Army unit on the 11th of October, 1993. This document, Mr. President, corresponds to a number of entries contained in the logbooks, which I referred to earlier in my remarks, the log books noting the names and numbers of prisoners taken out of the Heliodrom by various units. We have reviewed those logbooks and we find entries in several of them memorialising the fact that HV Croatian Army units routinely often used prisoners from the Heliodrom for forced labour. Those entries are found in Exhibit 566.2, 567.1, and in particular, a number of entries are found in Exhibit 645.1, which includes explicit references to the Tigrovi and the Gromovi, the tigers and the thunders, units of the HV which the Trial Chamber has heard from several witnesses were based at the Heliodrom. Finally, on this point, Mr. President, we ask the Trial Chamber to recall the testimony of Defence expert witness, Mr. Davor Marijan, who indicated that during the second half of 1993, there were members of the HV 1st, 2nd, 5th, and 7th Guards Brigades present in the territory of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, those being the Tigrovi, Gromovi, and the 7th guards Brigade being the Pumas. It's our submission, Mr. President, that the evidence establishes beyond a reasonable doubt that Croatian Army units participated directly in the conflict which the Trial Chamber is concerned with, in this case. They were present in terms of numbers, men, materiel, support. Their presence was noted by witnesses, victims who were present in the Heliodrom, witnesses who were taken by members of the HV out to perform forced labour in positions all across western Herzegovina, by the sightings and findings of the international community, representatives who were present in the region, and all of those documents are found among the IAC materials which have been submitted into evidence. Mr. President, it's our submission that this evidence proves the direct participation of Croatia in this conflict beyond a reasonable doubt, and that that presence and that participation in this conflict means that the conflict in which all of these crimes occurred, all of the crimes committed by Vinko Martinovic and by Mladen Naletilic, are crimes that occurred in the context of an international armed conflict. It's our submission therefore that all of the grave breaches charged under article 2 of the statute apply, the requirements have been met. I've finished my comments, Mr. President, it's been my honour to appear before the Trial Chamber in this case and to make these closing submissions. At this time, I'd like to give the floor back to Mr. Scott so that he can continue to address the additional submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, I'm going to continue on some of the other aspects of what might be called the political international armed conflict and the existence of a broader plan, if you will, the widespread and systematic character of the conduct that was carried out by the HDZ and the HVO throughout the time in question. We have covered these matters at great detail in our brief in a history that begins in at least 1991, if not sooner, and talks about the evolution of these political forces and showing in our submission quite clearly that at the end of the day, Mr. President, Your Honours, the HVO and the HDZ political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina was nothing less or more than the alter ego of the Tudjman government and of the HDZ political party in Zagreb. In short, Your Honours, it's the Prosecution position, and we submit to you that the evidence establishes it, there was indeed commencing in at least 1991, and thereafter, a plan for what might be called a greater Croatia, just as Slobodan Milosevic had his vision, he and others around him had his vision for a greater Serbia, the evidence shows that Franjo Tudjman and those around him, both in Croatia itself and in Herceg-Bosna, had their vision of a Greater Croatia. The Chamber heard evidence throughout the trial of the Croatian banovina that existed at least as of 1939 and how indeed the banovina provided the model for Herceg-Bosna and very briefly, Mr. President, we would suggest that in addition to all the other testimonial and documentary evidence, that the banovina provided the model for Herceg-Bosna and in fact was mentioned a number of times by Franjo Tudjman himself, that at the end of the day, all one really needs to do is take a map of Herceg-Bosna and a map of the banovina - all those maps are in evidence and the exact numbers are in our brief - and simply lay one on top of the other and you will see that Herceg-Bosna, for all practical purposes, was the banovina. I'm going to in the time remaining highlight only two parts, really one part on two separate occasions, of the widespread and systematic plan for establishing Herceg-Bosna and for either removing the Muslim population from Herceg-Bosna or relegating it to such a secondary role that, for all practical purposes, Herceg-Bosna had become a Croat state. The parts that I'm going to focus on out of the many aspects covered in our brief is the two ultimatums. The Prosecution would submit Your Honours, does submit, that there can be little stronger proof than the existence of two ultimatums both given and both acted upon when the Muslims did not do what the HVO wanted them to do. If we might compare this to a more, hate to say typical murder case but to a domestic murder case, it is as if you have the accused who tells the victim on such and such a day, unless you do what I want you to do, I am going to kill you. And when in fact the victim doesn't do what the accused wanted him or her to do, he carries out that intention. It is powerful evidence of intent and at the existence of a plan. Both of these ultimatums relate back to what the Chamber has heard considerable evidence about, and that is the so-called Vance-Owen Peace Plan. I'm going to treat this matter much more -- in a much more abbreviated way than in our brief, but the highlights are these: The Vance-Owen Plan was conceived in late 1992 and it was continued to be in discussions until at least the spring of 1993. In a nutshell, it proposed a democratically elected arrangement of multi-ethnic provinces, while indeed a bona fide ethnic majority might expect to have some democratic advantages just as one would find in a one-person one-vote system. The Vance-Owen proposal properly understood, Your Honours, never meant in the Prosecution's submission, and I suggest in the international community, never meant anything like exclusive government power by one ethnic group. However, that is how the Croats and the HVO and the HDZ attempted to enforce it. For whatever reason, and for these purposes the reasons are not important, maybe it was sheer good luck, but for whatever reason, the Croats had received generally favourable treatment under the Vance-Owen proposals. The Croats representing approximately 17 and a half per cent of the overall population of Bosnia and Herzegovina were to be allocated -- again in their view of things, were to be allocated approximately 28 per cent of the territory. It was because of this, in fact, favourable treatment, that the saying began to be circulated around this time in Zagreb and in Bosnia, that what HVO really stood for was hvala Vance-Owen, meaning thank you, Vance-Owen. Given the favourable numbers and their interpretation of Vance-Owen, Tudjman and the Herceg-Bosna leadership immediately endorsed it and saw it as a tool to indeed accomplish the banovina which I mentioned to the Chamber a moment ago. And again, when you look at Vance-Owen provinces 8 and 10 and compare those to the historic borders of the banovina, you will see the great similarity of the two. By mid-January, 1993, the HDZ, HVO leadership was so eager in fact to implement their vision of Vance-Owen, that they refused to wait longer and issued an ultimatum to the Muslims to accept their view of what the plan involved. On the 15th of January, 1993, HVO president Jadranko Prelec announced that all units of the BH Army currently in regions 3, 8 and 10 which were proclaimed Croatian in the Geneva arrangements are subordinate to the command of the main headquarters of the HVO armed forces. This was immediately turned into an ultimatum with a deadline of the 20th of January, 1993, when Prelec says the decision shall be implemented within five days starting from today, 15 January, 1993. Well, the Chamber knows from the evidence that it has received that as the 20th of January approached and then passed, the first major armed confrontations between the Muslims and the Croat armed forces since Prozor in October 1992, these major clashes broke out in various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including at Gornji Vakuf and in Busovaca. Mr. President, the international observers on the ground at the time were unanimous in their conclusion that these conflicts were brought about for one reason and one reason only, reported in part in Exhibit P230, an UN -- an UNPROFOR report of the 24th of January, 1993, where it simply characterised the HVO conduct as a premature -- and I'm quoting,"a premature and imperfect grab for control." That was -- led to the January and early February conflicts. Things managed to calm down a bit. There continued to be localised clashes but nothing on a large scale until the events in mid-April, 1993 that the Chamber has heard so much about. The Vance-Owen negotiations continued and on the 25th of March, 1993, President Izetbegovic of Bosnia-Herzegovina signed the Vance-Owen Plan, including the map which is shown in Exhibit 239.1 at page 280. Now, it's been a bone of contention in this trial for some time, virtually I suppose since the first day, that something was said, that some commitment was made by the Bosnian side, by Izetbegovic, that somehow justified what the HVO did thereafter. And Mr. President, the Prosecution's position on this has been consistent throughout, and we detailed the evidence in our brief. There was nothing in the Vance-Owen Plan signed by Izetbegovic that committed the Bosnian government to any sort of plan or arrangement as that interpreted by the HVO. In fact, it's very clear and there is one sentence at page 280 of the treaty or of the plan signed by Izetbegovic under the heading, "Withdrawal of forces," and it says simply this: "Both Bosnian army and HVO forces shall be deployed, both, in provinces 5, 8, 9 and 10, most importantly for our purposes, 8 and 10, under arrangements agreed between them." End of Vance-Owen. Now, again, as they did in January, the HVO and the HDZ was so anxious to enforce their view of what all this meant that Mate Boban or someone for him, surely, prepared a proposed joint statement dated the 2nd of April which Boban quickly signed and proposed for Izetbegovic to sign which allegedly would have put into effect the subordination of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina units to the HVO in provinces 8 and 10. It's the Prosecution submission, Your Honour, and we submit there is no evidence to the contrary, that President Izetbegovic never signed Boban's proposed joint statement, and there was never such an agreement. In fact, when one looks at Exhibit P272, which is a record -- excuse me, 273.1, my apology, is a record of an HVO cabinet meeting on the 3rd of April, the day after Boban's proposed statement and the very content of the minutes of the meeting make it clear as of that time, there was no joint statement, and they talk about that and they talk about well if Izetbegovic doesn't sign, we are going to enforce Vance-Owen anyway. It's very clear that the minutes can be read one way and one way only, and that is that as of 3rd of April, there was no such agreement, and in fact, there never was. As further evidence of that, the Chamber can look to the presidential transcript PT 8.1, a high level meeting in Zagreb on the 24th of April, including Tudjman, Izetbegovic, Boban, Lord Owen and others, and it's very clear we submit, Your Honours, to anyone reading that transcript, that there was no agreement or commitment by Izetbegovic and in fact it becomes very clear, there was never a meeting of the minds at all. And in our papers we essentially submit that what really becomes clear in that transcript, although Vance-Owen lingered on for some weeks thereafter is that for all practical purposes Vance-Owen was dead. Finally the Defence expert, Mladen Ancic himself a Defence expert confirmed that Izetbegovic never signed the joint statement. The ultimatum's, Mr. President, Judge Clark, Judge Diarra, are powerful evidence of the HVO plan and the HVO intention. I want to turn the bulk of the -- my remaining comments to the political aspects, if you will, of the international armed conflict. Mr. Stringer has talked about, if you will, the involvement of the Croatian armed forces, the Croatian Army, on the ground, and that is indeed under the Tribunal jurisprudence one of the ways to establish the existence of an international armed conflict. As we've made clear in our brief, Mr. President, there is also an alternative way, and that is to establish the overall control of one state on an organisation or quasi -- one might say, in this instance, quasi-state elsewhere, leading to the that the foreign state is in fact completely in charge or effectively controlling the other entity. Even if for whatever reason, and we submit that the evidence would not support another conclusion, but for whatever reason, if the evidence on direct HV participation on the ground were not to persuade the Chamber, Your Honour, the evidence is overwhelming that the HVO, the HDZ, and the leadership thereof was nothing other than the alter ego of the Tudjman government and the HDZ party in Zagreb. There was overall control. And in the documents that I'll show you, take the Chamber through in the last few minutes, we submit is compelling evidence of exactly that. I told the Chamber in my earlier remarks that I would present my part of the argument by calling upon six witnesses, and I took the Chamber through five. And I now call the sixth witness, and I call as our sixth witness, Franjo Tudjman. With Mr. Bos's assistance, I would like to direct the Chamber's attention, the courtroom's attention, to a compilation of presidential transcripts which should be at the back, virtually at the back of the bundle, our binder, that the Chamber has, and Mr. Bos again has a complete set that he will try and follow me on the ELMO with. It's in the back of -- I'm told it's in the back of what's called label part 1. Mr. President, just so you know, for ease of reference and to have a unique page number instead of referring constantly to the so-called R numbers, we now have just a regular page -- continuous page document, 75 pages, excerpts of four presidential transcripts, PT 12, I think 13, 14 and PT 28 have been -- excerpts of those transcripts have been merged into one document. Of course, the Chamber has the full and complete transcripts in evidence, and this is simply as an aid to assist argument on these matters. What the Prosecution submits, Your Honours, is that going through these documents and that is all the transcripts -- all the presidential transcripts, but in particular these four, it becomes abundantly clear that Croatia exercised overall control on Herceg-Bosna, on the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on the HVO. What becomes clear is that throughout both the transcripts and the other evidence that the Prosecution has submitted, Mate Boban was essentially hand-picked by Franjo Tudjman and he was removed by Franjo Tudjman in late 1993 when the pressure of the international community became so great that, if you will, Mate Boban was jettisoned because he'd become too much of a lightning rod in bringing too much pressure to bear on the Republic of Croatia. And Tudjman said to his good friend Mate, Sorry, Mate, it's time for you to go. Beyond that, the Croatian government specifically Franjo Tudjman and his immediate circle, hand-picked or approved the government of Herceg-Bosna, shown in these transcripts. Further, Franjo Tudjman and those around him, hand-picked and approved the -- virtually the entire HVO general staff. Referenced -- or shown in part by the document that Mr. Stringer showed you a few moments ago, Exhibit 664.2, which I will come back to. What I'd like to do, Mr. President, is spend some moments and it will take sometime, but this will be the bulk of my remaining comments other than a few closing remarks. But in looking at these presidential transcripts, we can see those things which I've indicated to the Chamber in the last few minutes. Starting in the very -- page 1, we have a meeting on the 9th of November, 1993, between Franjo Tudjman, the President of the Republic of Croatia, and representatives of Herceg-Bosna, this particular meeting taking place in Split. And Mate Boban goes on to say, From all their political in central Bosnia they proposed and set Ante Valenta as a candidate of other Croats, Mr. Zubak, but to put him strictly in charge of justice and administration. Kresimir Zubak managed to say, To put him in charge only for the portfolio of justice and administration. Admittedly, that particular entry is somewhat garbled, but if you put it in the context of all that followed it's quite clear. Then on the next page Mr. Boban goes on and talks about well, How about the 4th vice-president? How about Vlado Sucic? There are other proposals and in fact about the middle of page 2, Boban says, Well, let's give this man Alic, he's a Muslim, as his deputy. We will give him a Muslim for a deputy, that Muslim is not all that important. And so on. And then, By the way, Bruno Stojic stays on as Minister of Defence. Going to page three, How about education, schooling, and the rest? Jozo Maric nominated for that position. You see at the bottom of that page, again, talking about President Tudjman to tell you, here is 15 people from Croatia and you assigned them. Mate Boban on page 4: "We have ten people, making a government of ten people, which is basically a government drawing on the process, model, manner, decrees, laws of the Croatian state and there's no need to invent anything regarding the organisation of authority." Skipping to page 7, coming quickly to the end of the excerpts of that particular transcript which is PT 12, talks about proposing Dario Kordic to a senior position. Further on that page, the Croatian consulate general, at least if not at that time, later, Ciro Grubisic being proposed and Milan Kovac. The Chamber may recall that Milan Kovac was a Defence witness here being proposed by the inner circle for a senior position in the Herceg-Bosna government. Exhibit PT 13. An amazing display, Mr. President, Your Honours, of Franjo Tudjman's direct, hands-on involvement at the most detailed level of the affairs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Specific actions what's happening there, what should happen there. A meeting on the 6th of November in the presidential palace in Zagreb, Tudjman says, "[It's] clear that the Muslims will go - they said Travnik, and they took Travnik, that then, and accordingly we'll be reduced to just Western Herzegovina. Right until now, in June I called the Minister and the Chief of Headquarters, and at the beginning of July I asked, I told them, in Bosnia-Herzegovina war is now being waged for the area of the border of the Croatian state. Accordingly, one has to do everything to help this -- one has to, excuse me -- one has to do everything to help this area hold out. It is not the same to us whether the...Croatian state, that is, will Jajce...or with Travnik -- with Travnik, only would no be Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca. In diplomatic talks we have not given up on Kiseljak and Kresovo." Franjo Tudjman talking in detail about the borders of the Croatian state including municipalities in Herzegovina in central Bosnia. Page 10, first paragraph start being on that page, President Tudjman talking, "We had to do all this, of course under the cover of sending volunteers. But gentlemen from the Ministry and the Minister and the Chief of the Main Headquarters, people say correctly that when we brought, they did not get this help from Croatia in time, and so because of it being late they lost. Let's say they now say that the Muslims hold here these regions that..." I might submit, Your Honour, the Prosecution would submit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- if one reads enough of these transcripts, you can virtually see Tudjman and the others pouring over a map, talking about borders, talking about this place and that place, detailed events on the ground in a foreign state. This is not a military -- in fact right here he says this is not a military map. What we are working with here, gentlemen, this is not a military map, but they can mainly serve -- the Muslims can mainly hold a high land and mountain region. Talks about negotiation with the Serbs in the next paragraph. "The Serbs hold Kupres, the Serbs agreed that in the demarcation this comes into our region, with the proviso that here we gave up on all those areas that were Croatian..." A trade. A trade with Serbs for territory of a foreign state, a state recognised by the international community, a member state of the United Nations called Bosnia and Herzegovina. Talks about on top of page 11, in detail, We couldn't hold on to some parts of central Bosnia, it's too attenuated, Vares is too far out there. We would like to hold on to it, but militarily it's not practical. We couldn't hold on. At the bottom of page 11, he talks about the compactness of the territory. Compactness of territory, that is what we have to ensure, Novi Travnik, Busovaca, what we have achieved by the demarcation agreement, but now I would have a go -- Tudjman apparently is feeling bullish this day. He says, Well, let's have a go at Kresovo as well. We'll see what will happen. Bottom of page 12, Accordingly all you in the ministry in the headquarters, are you quite clear about that? This is the question of the borders of the Croatian state, the future of the Croatian state. Accordingly, make things possible for General Roso. Now this is dated the 6th of November and Roso had either just gone or was about to go to take over as chief of the HVO general staff. So Tudjman is saying make things possible for General Roso, give him all the help and manpower. For now, it has to be on the basis of volunteers. I'm not sure that tomorrow if we went on that we won't have to confront them directly, but for the moment under the cover of volunteers. Page 15, Janko Bobetko, the chief of the general -- of the Croatian Army, mentioned by Mr. Stringer, goes on and has a discussion with President Tudjman and others of detailed tactical matters. These aren't broad political statements, these are on the ground, this is what's happening, this is what we have to do in Bosnia. Bobetko defends his actions,. "We have analysed things five times, and not once have they been obeyed [down there], they have done things their own way. Well, that's water under the bridge. I personally think the key matter is to take Gornji Vakuf. President Tudjman: I said that just now, don't let's repeat that. Of course is a key matter." And then they get on through another series of steps, the blockading of Bugojno, the formation -- the further reorganisation of the armed forces. Bottom of page 15, "Fourthly, we have to find solutions to group our forces, that idea of volunteers, let that stay, please, it is the most legal, the most efficient, but a command has to be created that will give enough authority and knowledge for us to execute it...In the next eight days we have to take Gornji Vakuf." Chamber can skim some of these pages for itself. Janko Bobetko says to Tudjman on 16, "You appointed General Roso." You Franjo Tudjman, appointed the chief of the HVO main staff. You appointed General Roso. If Roso taking on -- is Roso taking on that responsibility? A guarantee to execute this? Because we do not have any time. What will happen if things go the other way around? And then there again they continue on the liquidation of Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf. Page 30 -- or excuse me page 20. Mr. Stringer told you a few moments ago about the appointment of Tole, Zarko Tole, a senior HV officer to the HVO main staff in approximately August. Here we are now in November, early November, a couple of months, several months later, and what is President Tudjman saying? Yesterday, Tole, I think said -- we must impress upon the Chamber the detail of what's -- President Tudjman is involved in daily communications informed of daily communications of what is happening in the military situation on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Yesterday, Tole, I said they can undertake some local action where, by Dreznica, yes, and by Jablanica, yes, on the plateau. Then they talk about Mostar. Page 23, the middle of the page again talking we got to take Gornji Vakuf and we have the assessments of Tole and Praljak. By this time, Slobodan Praljak is either still in Bosnia or has maybe just come back to Zagreb early November, 1993. They talk about helicopter flights and in the documents in evidence, the Chamber may, if it has time, and we know we have given you a large volume of material, but you will see UNPROFOR reports and ECMM reports for months during 1992, 1993, where they would see helicopter flights. In UNPROFOR and the ECMM were trying for the life of them trying to figure out where were these helicopters coming from? Well, Mr. President, the problem -- the mystery is solved. On page 23, they talk about the helicopter flights. Toward the bottom of the page, They carried out 20 flights in the recent period in impossible conditions to Vitez in central Bosnia. It even talks about the extreme situations, as at that time Vitez was an enclave, the helicopters had to take off from Grude. And he goes on. I won't take the time to go through detail. Where were the helicopters coming from? Whose helicopters were they? The Croatian Army's. Page 25, Janko Bobetko says: "The first battalion that went had 780 men with all the artillery. That was the most elite unit that we sent. Mr. Davor Marijan comes in and tells the Chamber, there were no units, there were no HV units in Bosnia, maybe some individuals, maybe some volunteer soldiers, no units. Mr. President, that's not what Janko Bobetko says. Top of page 26, Janko Bobetko: "A political and strategic change will come that moment we take Gornji Vakuf." Janko Bobetko further down the page: "That is the spot that has to be taken. It settles everything." Mr. President, I'm going to go very quickly now, because page -- the point is this, Mr. President: Those kind of discussions go on page after page after page of the presidential transcripts. You also see Tudjman, I suppose not unlike other political leaders incredibly concerned about PR. And bad press for the Republic of Croatian. On top of page 33, he talks about having read the latest issue of Newsweek. He talks about the events in Stupni Do. What happened down there? This looks terrible for us. Who is this man Ivica Rajic? And they, Boban knows and tells them, it's Ivica Rajic, it's one of our guys. And Tudjman is having a fit for the impact that these matters have on the state of Croatia. Now going on skipping down to page 36 we come back again -- my apologies to translation. Page 36 and thereafter, simply say this: They then pick up in this particular series of meetings, the appointment of the government for Herceg-Bosna. Some of the names the Chamber may well recognise. How about Zulfo Robovic, the bottom of page 36, the Muslim democratic party. That's theirs, that's a suggestion both Poharin and Mostar. President Tudjman: "When we're discussing a Muslim from Mostar, what, why are you giving him precedence over Hadziosmanovic?" That Zulfo from the very first day -- Mate Boban, on page 37, that Zulfo from the very first day when the SDA did not want to participate in our government, he was in electric power industry and he stayed, and so forth. And then Tudjman goes off on a tangent. They are talking about appoints the the government of Herzegovina Herceg-Bosna and he says: "By the way, that bridge in Mostar, who destroyed it?" Well, Mate Boban says it was fired on before and it was raining a lot, so it collapsed on its own. President Tudjman: "Are we going to be accused again? It goes on for some time talking about the bridge. Then they return to appointing the government. On page 41, you will see the name Bagaric. Head of the HVO medical corps. Someone the Chamber heard from. Being discussed and hand-picked by Franjo Tudjman. Page 42, the involvement of Ivic Pasalic one of President Tudjman's strongest, closest advisers, also a Defence witness in this case. Of course Mr. Pasalic didn't like the presidential transcripts, of course he doesn't like them because he doesn't like what they show. I'm going to skip down to page 47. The Chamber has seen this one before. Again my apology. It's both a function of the time and a function of reading, I'm an afraid but I will try to slow down. The Chamber has seen this transcript. The most important part of it is the discussion of this Exhibit 664.2. Mr. President, Judge Clark, Judge Diarra, the events in this transcript literally come alive off the page. You almost -- almost -- feel sorry for Bobetko for the grilling he's getting from Franjo Tudjman. Who could have created a document like that that proves we have appointed the entire HVO general staff? Tell me, General Bobetko, please explain to me how could a document like that have been created? It goes on for pages. This proves exactly what we've been denying all along. We said they were volunteers, whoever has this document knows we've been lying. Finally I'll go to Exhibit -- excuse me page 62, Exhibit PT 28, this transcript serves two purposes. One is it continues what I've said a few moments ago the detailed involvement of President Franjo Tudjman in the day-to-day events on the ground in Bosnia, and this transcript has the additional aspect of directly touching upon the two accused in this case. I'm going to, because of time, again skip to -- on page 64 and 65 they are talking about some trouble they are having with Kvesic, the Minister of Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And Tudjman essentially says, Well, we got rid of Boban and if we have to we'll get rid of Kvesic as well. Going to page 66, obvious concerns about what's happening in Mostar. The President: "Tell me, please, those names which, as we have seen, are also circulating in diplomatic circles, do you still have them,...what is the third name? (Baja)." To an unknown speaker at that particular moment: "There are two, but it shouldn't be connected with the wrong one, we have a Baja, an extraordinary Commander of the 2nd Company, and we have a Baja there, but it's a different, as you know," (Milicevic, Baja Milicevic, there is also Martinovic). President: "All right, what about them, where are they? These two are in Mostar, as far as I know, this Stela and this Baja, that Milicevic, they are in Mostar." And it goes on. Again go back to talking about Kvesic, For two years he's been carrying out his duty. He served the master. Bottom of page 69, we are quickly coming to the end. Susak says: "Mr. President, let us agree on the Tuta case. I both do link him with others and I don't. Everything in Siroki Brijeg, everything that was shot at, those were Tuta's men who were shot at, Tuta's best fighters. Culjo Andaba -- the Prosecution submits Andaba is Andabak -- Andaba is Tuta's deputy." This is what the Defence Minister of Croatia -- he doesn't seem to have any doubt about it. Andaba is Tuto's deputy. In all the shooting in Siroki Brijeg, those are Tuta's men. The President: "This now?" Page 72: "I would like to conclude, Mr. President, an assessment should be made now. The things Tuta did and did not carry out, all witnesses are here. With the exception of Tuta, we do not have a person for military activities in the area of Herceg-Bosna. I think that it was recognised unilaterally by everybody, that Tuta is a little...and that is the factor. Do we have to come up with a judgement that is opportunistic to put him in jail. I think it is not, you people who are in the field, I think it is good." And Susak goes on to say: I will hide him here for some time, if he going down -- is he going to return down there, but I do not think order can be established putting Tuta. "Tuta should not be in prison now, he should be hidden..." President Tudjman: "Then, Tuta should be kept in Zagreb, but not in Herzegovina either. Susak: "He must not enter Herzegovina, Mr. President, he must disappear. President Tudjman: But if he is in Makarska, it is only an hour drive to Herzegovina, that's not good." Top of page 74 they turn their attention to Andabak. He's a good soldier, Mr. President, he was carrying out -- he's carrying out orders. Mr. President, that speaks volumes about the overall control of Franjo Tudjman, his government, his circle, of the events in Bosnia. The Prosecution submits that it's abundantly clear that there was an international armed conflict in which Croatia was directly and extensively involved. Turning to my concluding remarks, Mr. President, and I will, I'm confident, conclude before 7.00. And I'd like to give my apology again to translation for the speed. I apologise for that. Mr. President, Your Honours, I'd like to close with this. The Prosecution's submission. The world knows that horrific crimes and tremendous human suffering occurred in the wars concerning the former Yugoslavia, including the Croat-Muslim war in 1993, 1994. Sadly, it was during that conflict that a new term was coined, a new term came into usage, an ugly term called "ethnic cleansing." There were victims on all sides of the war and as the Prosecutor told you on the first day and will tell you again on the last day, we defend no criminals in that war, we support all victims, be they Muslim, Croat, or Serb. There were certainly victims on all sides; there were crimes on all sides. Much has been said and written about these events and about the political and social force that is led to them. Much has been said and written about people like Milosevic and Tudjman and Boban and others. Mr. President, Judge Clark, Judge Diarra, it must never be forgotten, however, that without people like Naletilic, Tuta, senior commanders and operatives, without people like Martinovic, Stela, willing and able to carry out events on the ground, without those people, people like Milosevic and Tudjman can't commit these crimes. It's the people like Tuta and Stela who order, participate in, and condone the expulsion of families and the plunder of their property, the beating, torture, mistreatment of human beings taken prisoner, or arrested, merely because they were the wrong ethnic group. The crimes and the victims of Naletilic and Martinovic cry out for justice to be done. I'm sure if this Chamber was sitting in Mostar, this gallery would be packed with victims who would have very physical and direct way be appealing to this Chamber for justice. The Prosecution submits that based on the law, based on the evidence that it submitted to this Chamber, we have proven our case. We pray, based on the law and the evidence, that the accused be convicted on all the charges against them. The Chamber saw this poster during the trial. It's Exhibit 639 -- I'm sorry, 939. Photograph of Tuta and in Serbo-Croatian language saying, "Our victory." This is the man that Martin Garrod, Sir Martin, said he was considered a war hero by so many. A man his soldiers looked up to. And unfortunately so many of them followed into misconduct of the most egregious kind. I'm going to ask Mr. Bos to put on the ELMO Exhibit 43. I want the Chamber to consider the poster of Mr. Naletilic and at the same time the photograph that is on the ELMO. This is a photograph Exhibit 43 it's admitted in evidence, it's a photo of the Emir Obradovic family, Emir Obradovic was killed on the 17th of September in Mostar, a Muslim. But that's not why the photograph is used for this purpose. I submit to you, Mr. President, Judge Clark, Judge Diarra, this is instead photograph of any family. It doesn't matter if they were Croat or Muslim or Serb. These are the people who this war tore apart. And as we said a moment ago, there were victims on all sides. Look at this man who was killed, whose two children, a wife, how many -- how many wives and children, their father is missing, killed, never came home. How many mothers were expelled, that were kicked out of their house, they got a boot in the back as one of the witness testified she got from Stela, how many women thrown out of their flats in Mostar? How many lost their husbands and their sons and their daughters? The children, how many were killed? How many were starved during the siege of Mostar? How many died in Mostar because they couldn't get basic medical care because the HVO blocked access to the town? How many of their mothers their fathers and brothers never came home? Maybe their father survived the war, but even now that isn't quite right. The child looks at the mother and asks her father, Why does mom cry so often? What Naletilic and Martinovic wanted was all the power and none of the responsibility. Based on the law and the evidence, Your Honours, don't let them have his victory, don't let them have their victory. The law and the evidence shows that these two men are guilty. Justice must be done. We ask they be convicted on all counts. We ask that Naletilic be sentenced to a term of at least 35 years imprisonment and that Stela be imprisoned to a term of lot less than 25 years. Thank you very much.
